title: Mathematics Foundations: Discover, Prove, Compute
description: A first-principles mathematics course with connected mathematician, mathematics programmer, and computational hacker pathways. Learners move from concrete examples to representations, conjectures, code, counterexamples, and proof.

modules.title: Mathematics programmer pathway
modules.description: Represent ideas as algorithms, tests, and reproducible computation.

modules.title: Computational hacker pathway
modules.description: Decompose a problem, build a minimal implementation, debug, test, and explain.

objectives.title: Whole-number structure and additive patterns
objectives.description: Recognize order, parity, and additive sequences; state the domain of a general pattern.

objectives.title: Variables and algebraic expressions
objectives.description: Represent changing quantities and relationships with variables and expressions.

objectives.title: Divisibility and factor pairs
objectives.description: Use exact grouping and factor pairs to reason about divisibility.

objectives.title: Prime numbers and primality
objectives.description: Classify prime numbers, form conjectures, and implement bounded primality checks.

objectives.title: Algorithmic loops and repeated computation
objectives.description: Model repeated operations with state, update rules, and termination conditions.

objectives.title: Euclid's proof of the infinitude of primes
objectives.description: Construct a proof by contradiction using a finite list and a product-plus-one argument.

objectives.title: Finite experiments and counterexamples
objectives.description: Use bounded computation to discover patterns and refute universal conjectures without mistaking finite tests for proof.

lessons.title: Discover counting patterns
lessons.body: Begin with concrete groups and growing arrangements. Compare 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; notice the constant difference before writing a general rule.

stages.prompt: Arrange objects in a row, then add one more pair. What changes?
Compare 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9. Describe the change from one term to the next.
Draw the growing groups and identify what remains unchanged.
Explain why each new odd number is two more than the previous one.
Only after explaining the pattern, state the nth odd number as 2n − 1.

exercise.objective: Recognize additive structure and express a pattern in general form.
exercise.prompt: Find the 10th term of 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, ... State a rule for the nth odd number and verify it at three positions.
hints: Compare consecutive terms.
The difference is constant.
Start at 1 and add 2 for every step after the first.

rubric.description: Identifies the constant difference of two.
States a correct nth-term rule.
Checks at least three positions.

exercise.transfer_prompt: Start at 4 and add 3 each time. Give the nth-term rule and compare it with the odd-number rule.

lessons.title: Model a changing quantity
lessons.body: A jar begins with four coins and receives three more coins each minute. Build a table and describe the relationship before using a variable.

stages.prompt: Imagine a jar receiving one or more coins at a constant rate.
Record the amount after zero, one, two, three, and four minutes.
Plot elapsed time against the number of coins.
Explain the starting amount and the repeated increase.
Represent the relationship as 4 + 3m, defining m.

exercise.objective: Interpret a variable as a name for a changing or unknown quantity.
exercise.prompt: A jar starts with 4 coins and receives 3 more coins each minute. Make a table for the first five minutes and write a rule for the number of coins after m minutes.
hints: Separate the starting amount from the repeated increase.
The amount added is the same each minute.
A letter can stand for any allowed number of minutes.

rubric.description: Builds an accurate table.
Explains the starting amount and repeated increase.
Writes and interprets 4 + 3m.

exercise.transfer_prompt: Change the jar so it starts with 7 coins and receives 2 coins per minute. Write and explain the new rule.

lessons.title: Build a factor table
lessons.body: Arrange 12 counters into equal groups. Compare with 13 and 18, then use factor pairs to describe exact divisibility.

stages.prompt: Arrange 12 counters into equal rows without leftovers.
List row and column counts that use all 12 counters.
Repeat for 13 and 18 and compare the available arrangements.
Explain what it means for one number to divide another exactly.
Use factor-pair notation only after explaining the equal-group idea.

exercise.objective: Use divisibility and factor pairs to classify whole numbers.
exercise.prompt: For each integer from 1 through 30, list all positive factor pairs. Classify each number greater than 1 as prime or composite, and explain why 1 is neither.
hints: A factor pair multiplies to the target number.
Test possible divisors up to the square root; pairs then repeat in reverse.
A prime has exactly two positive factors.

rubric.description: Lists correct factor pairs.
Correctly classifies primes and composites.
Explains why 1 is neither prime nor composite.

exercise.transfer_prompt: Choose a composite number between 31 and 50, list all factor pairs, and justify that the list is complete.

lessons.title: Discover and test prime numbers
lessons.body: Explore prime numbers from factor pairs. Choose a mathematician activity (conjecture about remainders) or a programmer activity (implement a bounded prime checker), then compare what each kind of evidence establishes.

stages.prompt: Sort small-number cards into prime and composite groups using factor pairs.
List primes greater than 3 and below 50. Look for a repeated pattern.
Place each prime on a remainder wheel for division by 6.
Explain why a prime greater than 3 cannot be divisible by 2 or 3.
State the necessary form 6k − 1 or 6k + 1; explain why it is not sufficient.
For the programmer path, implement and test a divisor search bounded by the square root.

exercise.objective: Classify primes, form a conjecture, and implement a bounded primality test.
exercise.prompt: Choose one pathway activity: (A) list primes greater than 3 and below 50, compute remainders mod 6, and explain why finite examples are not a proof; or (B) write Python is_prime(n), handle n < 2, test 0, 1, 2, 9, 17, 49, and justify the square-root bound.
hints: A prime is greater than 1 and has no divisors other than 1 and itself.
If n has a factor larger than its square root, it has a paired factor below it.
For primes greater than 3, divisibility by 2 or 3 is impossible.

rubric.description: Uses the correct definition of prime and composite.
Explains the remainder condition or square-root factor-pair bound.
Uses accurate examples and states the limits of finite tests.

exercise.transfer_prompt: Find a composite number of the form 6k + 1 and explain why 6k ± 1 is necessary but not sufficient for primes greater than 3.

lessons.title: Build multiplication from repeated addition
lessons.body: Use equal groups and a running total to see multiplication as repeated addition, then implement a bounded loop.

stages.prompt: Make several equal groups of objects and count the total.
Write the same addend repeatedly and compare with the total.
Draw a counter that increases once for each group.
Explain the initial state, repeated update, and stopping condition.
Name the running total and number of repetitions.
Implement repeated addition with a loop, including zero and negative inputs.

exercise.objective: Represent multiplication as repeated addition and implement it with a loop.
exercise.prompt: Write multiply_by_addition(a, b) using a loop and repeated addition. Do not use the multiplication operator inside the function. Define behavior for zero and negative inputs and test at least five cases.
hints: For positive b, add a to a running total b times.
Start the running total at zero.
For negative b, count abs(b) repetitions and apply the sign.

rubric.description: Uses repeated addition and a loop.
Handles zero and negative inputs.
Includes at least five meaningful tests.

exercise.transfer_prompt: Explain how repeated addition relates to the distributive property and count the additions performed.

lessons.title: Prove there are infinitely many primes
lessons.body: Study Euclid's product-plus-one argument. The constructed number need not be prime: if it is composite, one of its prime divisors still lies outside the assumed complete list.

stages.prompt: Imagine someone claims to have written down every prime number.
Multiply the listed primes and add one. Examine the remainder when any listed prime divides the result.
Represent the product and the extra unit as a remainder argument.
Explain why no listed prime divides the new number.
Write N = p₁p₂...pₙ + 1 and derive the contradiction.

exercise.objective: Construct and explain Euclid's proof that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
exercise.prompt: Assume there are finitely many primes p₁ through pₙ. Construct N as their product plus one. Explain why no listed prime divides N, and why a prime divisor of N contradicts the complete-list assumption. Do not assume N itself is prime.
hints: Assume a finite complete list p₁, p₂, ..., pₙ.
Consider N = p₁p₂...pₙ + 1.
If N is composite, it still has a prime divisor; none of the listed primes divides it.

rubric.description: States the finite complete-list assumption.
Constructs the product-plus-one number.
Shows no listed prime divides the new number.
Uses a prime divisor to derive a contradiction.

exercise.transfer_prompt: Explain why the argument still works when the product-plus-one number is composite.

lessons.title: Find a counterexample to a conjecture
lessons.body: Search the Euler polynomial n² + n + 41 in increasing order. The first 40 values are prime, but n = 40 gives 1681 = 41². A single valid counterexample refutes the universal claim.

stages.prompt: Calculate n² + n + 41 for a few small values of n.
Record n, the polynomial value, and whether the value is prime.
Mark the first composite value on a number line or table.
Explain what a finite search can disprove and what it cannot prove.
State the tested domain and the universal claim precisely.
Write a bounded search that stops at the first counterexample and records its factorization.

exercise.objective: Use a finite computational search to find a counterexample and explain its scope.
exercise.prompt: Investigate the conjecture that n² + n + 41 is prime for every non-negative integer n. Search upward from zero, find the first counterexample, factor it, and state exactly what the finite search establishes.
hints: Start at n = 0 and increase by one.
Use the earlier primality checker or a separate divisor search.
At n = 40, the value is 1681 = 41 × 41.

rubric.description: Runs a reproducible finite search.
Finds n = 40 and factors 1681 as 41 × 41.
Explains the logical scope of the counterexample.

exercise.transfer_prompt: Replace 41 with 43 and search the first 50 non-negative integers. Explain what the result does and does not prove.
